lesson.title: Inside a Certificate: The X.509 Standard, Field by Field
lesson.summary: X.509 is the standardized data structure certificate authorities use to package an identity, a public key, and a validity window into a single signed document, which is why a certificate issued by any CA can be read and verified by any browser or server.
lesson.body:
A standard, in the general sense used throughout this unit, is a formally specified format that many independent implementations agree to follow so that they can interoperate without needing to coordinate directly with one another. Certificates are a perfect example of why that matters. If every certificate authority invented its own certificate format, no browser could reliably parse certificates issued by every CA it might encounter, and the entire chain of trust described in the previous chapter would collapse into a patchwork of incompatible formats. X.509, originally specified by the ITU-T and profiled for internet use in IETF RFC 5280, is the shared format that prevents that, and it is the reason a certificate from one CA, verified by software from a completely different vendor, just works.

An X.509 certificate carries a defined set of fields. The subject identifies who the certificate was issued to, for a website certificate this is typically a domain name. The issuer identifies which CA signed the certificate. The certificate carries the subject's public key itself, the whole point of the document being to bind that key to the identity above it. A validity period, expressed as a not before and a not after date, defines the window during which the certificate should be considered valid at all; checking whether right now falls inside that window is exactly why a verifying machine needs a reasonably accurate clock, tying directly back to the very first chapter in this unit on NTP. A serial number, unique to the issuing CA, identifies the certificate individually. The certificate also states which signature algorithm was used, and it carries extensions, most notably a Subject Alternative Name list enumerating every hostname the certificate is valid for, since a single certificate can cover more than one domain. Finally, and this is what makes the whole document meaningful rather than just a self-asserted claim, the certificate carries the CA's own digital signature computed over all of the fields above.

Here is what happens, concretely, when a browser validates a real certificate chain for example.com. Suppose the leaf certificate for example.com was signed by an intermediate called Example Intermediate CA, and the browser already has Example Root CA in its built in trust store. The browser first checks that the intermediate certificate is itself signed by a public key belonging to a root it already trusts. It then checks that the leaf certificate for example.com is signed by the intermediate's public key. It checks that the current date falls within the leaf's validity period. It checks that the hostname it is actually connecting to appears among the certificate's subject or Subject Alternative Names. Only once every one of those checks passes does the browser treat the public key inside the leaf certificate as genuinely belonging to example.com.

That entire sequence of checks is not something a user performs manually, it happens automatically, in milliseconds, at the very start of a TLS connection, which is exactly where the next two chapters pick up.
